order-and-disorder.idea: A solid need not have a repeating crystal pattern.
order-and-disorder.explanation: An ideal crystal repeats its atomic arrangement over long distances. An amorphous solid can be rigid without that long-range repetition. Real crystals also contain vibrations, surfaces and defects.

example.title: One repeating row
steps: Atoms lie at 0, 2, 4 and 6 nm in a toy row.
Moving the pattern by 2 nm aligns its interior positions with one another.

terms.definition: A structure with a repeating atomic pattern.
Without long-range crystal repetition.
Nanometre, one billionth of a metre.

lattice-basis-cell.idea: A crystal combines repeat positions with the same small pattern at each position.
lattice-basis-cell.explanation: The lattice gives the repeat positions. The basis is the group of atoms and their offsets placed at each one. Together they specify the ideal structure.

example.title: A two-atom repeating pattern
steps: Repeat every 0.6 nm with atoms at offsets 0 and 0.2 nm.
At repeat number two, the atoms are at 1.2 and 1.4 nm.

terms.definition: Repeat spacing.
Whole-number repeat label.
Atom's offset inside the repeating pattern.
The array of repeat positions.

planes-and-spacing.idea: Imagine a three-dimensional grid of atoms. You can draw sets of equally spaced flat slices through the grid in different directions.
planes-and-spacing.explanation: The slices are imaginary crystal planes. Three whole numbers, called Miller indices, name their orientation. In a cubic crystal, square these numbers, add them and take the square root. Divide the cube’s edge length by that result to find the spacing for that set of planes.

example.title: Diagonal planes in a cube
steps: For cube edge 0.40 nm, choose planes labeled (1,1,0).
Their spacing is 0.40/√2 ≈ 0.283 nm.

terms.definition: Whole-number labels describing crystal-plane orientation.
Cubic cell edge.
Spacing between the planes.

defects.idea: Different defects change different parts of a crystal's arrangement.
defects.explanation: A vacancy is a missing atom at a normal site. An interstitial is an atom in an extra position; a dislocation is a line where rows fail to match. Counting vacancies does not count all disorder.

example.title: Six empty sites
steps: Six of 2000 sites are vacant.
The vacancy fraction is 6/2000 = 0.003, or 0.3%.

terms.definition: An empty site in an otherwise occupied ideal pattern.
A line defect in the arrangement of atomic rows.

periodic-wave-phase.idea: Scattered waves reinforce when neighboring cells contribute matching phases.
periodic-wave-phase.explanation: Phase is a wave's stage in its repeating cycle. Neighboring crystal cells can send waves to the same point at matching stages, making a stronger signal. A whole-cycle difference still matches, which explains why certain scattering directions reinforce.

example.title: One full-cycle difference
steps: Let spacing a = 0.5 nm and wave-vector change q = 4π rad/nm.
Their product is 2π radians, one full phase turn.

terms.definition: Change in wave vector along the row, measuring the phase change per distance caused by scattering.
Cell spacing.
Any whole number.
A unit of angle; 2π radians make one full turn.
A change in motion, direction or wave pattern after an interaction. A detector can record how much goes in each direction.
A list of components that can be added and scaled together. A familiar example is a displacement arrow with length and direction.

reciprocal-lattice.idea: Reciprocal space maps repeating wave patterns rather than ordinary positions.
reciprocal-lattice.explanation: Its spacing is inversely related to the crystal's real-space spacing. A larger physical repeat therefore gives smaller reciprocal spacing. Inverse-length units describe wave patterns, not a second hidden crystal.

example.title: One crystal repeat
steps: A row repeats every 0.50 nm.
Its angular reciprocal spacing is 2π/0.50 = 4π rad/nm.

terms.definition: Reciprocal spacing in the angular wave-number convention.
Real-space repeat distance.
One divided by a number other than zero. The reciprocal of 4 is ¼.

bragg-condition.idea: Waves scattered by different layers of a crystal can line up and make a bright spot.
bragg-condition.explanation: A wavelength is the distance from one wave crest to the next. For the crests to line up, the extra distance travelled must be a whole number of wavelengths. The formula finds the angles where this can happen. Measure the angle from the layers. The arrangement of atoms can still cancel a spot.

example.title: One diffraction peak
steps: Use first order, wavelength 0.20 nm and θ = 30°.
The inferred plane spacing is 0.20 nm; the beam-to-beam scattering angle is 60°.

terms.definition: Plane spacing.
Diffraction order, a whole number.
Wavelength.
Angle between ray and planes.
The spreading of a wave when it passes through an opening or around an edge.
A change in motion, direction or wave pattern after an interaction. A detector can record how much goes in each direction.
The distance along a wave from one point to the matching point in the next cycle, such as crest to crest.

diffraction-inference.idea: For the same reflection and wavelength, a larger diffraction angle means smaller plane spacing.
diffraction-inference.explanation: Rearrange the Bragg rule: spacing is inversely related to sinθ. Compare the same indexed reflection each time. This detects a spacing change without identifying its cause.

example.title: A shifting reflection
steps: With nλ = 0.30 nm, sinθ rises from 0.50 to 0.60.
The spacing falls from 0.30 nm to 0.25 nm.

terms.definition: A particular identified set of crystal planes producing a diffraction peak.
The spreading of a wave when it passes through an opening or around an edge.
The distance along a wave from one point to the matching point in the next cycle, such as crest to crest.

bond-equilibrium.idea: Near a stable bond length, a small displacement produces a restoring force.
bond-equilibrium.explanation: Potential energy has a minimum at the resting separation. Its slope determines force. A local spring model can describe small changes, but cannot be extended to arbitrarily large stretching.

example.title: A slightly stretched bond
steps: Use stiffness 40 N/m and stretch 0.01 nm, or 10⁻¹¹ m.
The local force is −4 × 10⁻¹⁰ N, pulling toward smaller separation.

terms.definition: Small-displacement stiffness.
Equilibrium separation.
A force pointing back toward the resting position.
Energy associated with an arrangement, such as the height of a weight above the floor.
How much a graph rises or falls for each step to the right.

bond-types.idea: Bond labels describe how electrons help hold a material together.
bond-types.explanation: Ionic bonding emphasizes attraction between charged ions. Covalent bonding emphasizes shared electron states between neighbors. Metallic bonding includes states extending across many atoms. Real materials can combine these features.

example.title: A hydrogen-molecule bond picture
steps: In a simple hydrogen-molecule model, two electrons occupy a shared bonding pattern between two nuclei.
This is covalent bonding: the shared electron distribution helps hold the nuclei together rather than assigning each electron to a separate atom.

terms.definition: An atom or group with net electric charge.
Bonding involving shared electronic states between atoms.
Bonding involving electronic states spread across many atoms.

stress-strain.idea: Compare stretching using force per area and extension per original length.
stress-strain.explanation: Stress is force divided by area; strain is extension divided by starting length. In a small, reversible linear stretch, their ratio is Young's modulus. Stiffness is different from breaking strength.

example.title: A stretched wire
steps: A 20 N pull acts over 2 × 10⁻⁶ m², giving stress 10⁷ Pa.
With modulus 10¹¹ Pa and starting length 0.50 m, the extension is 0.05 mm.

terms.definition: Force per area.
Extension divided by initial length.
The stiffness ratio for a specified small uniaxial stretch.
One amount divided by another. Three red counters for every two blue gives a red-to-blue ratio of 3/2.

elastic-limits.idea: A material can be stiffer in one direction than another.
elastic-limits.explanation: Elastic means the deformation reverses when the load is removed. Linear means stress is proportional to strain, an extra assumption. A single stiffness value applies only to the specified direction and loading conditions.

example.title: One direction of a crystal
steps: A stress of 100 MPa gives strain 0.001 in the linear range.
The inferred Young's modulus in that direction is 100 GPa.

terms.definition: Stress.
Strain.
One million pascals.
One billion pascals.
Dependence on direction.
Two quantities are proportional when multiplying one by a certain factor multiplies the other by that same factor.
Something you take as true for a calculation, such as assuming that a cart’s speed stays steady.

lattice-displacements.idea: An atom's neighbors help determine its restoring force.
lattice-displacements.explanation: In a simple spring-linked row, unequal displacements stretch the connecting springs. The force depends on differences between neighbors, not absolute position. Moving the whole row equally would stretch no springs.

example.title: One displaced atom
steps: The central mass moves 0.01 nm while its two neighbors remain still.
The spring-force bracket is −0.02 nm, so the force pulls it back.

terms.definition: Displacement from equilibrium.
Nearest-neighbor spring stiffness.

acoustic-optical.idea: Atoms in one repeating cell can move together or against each other.
acoustic-optical.explanation: A vibration pattern is called a mode. In a long-wavelength pattern, moving neighboring cells together barely stretches their bonds, so its frequency approaches zero. Two atoms inside each cell can instead move against each other and keep stretching a bond, allowing a nonzero frequency.

example.title: Opposite motion inside a cell
steps: In a two-atom cell, one atom moves right while the other moves left.
Their bond stretches, so this repeated internal motion can oscillate at a finite frequency.

terms.definition: A family of vibration patterns whose frequency approaches zero as wavelength grows.
A family that can retain nonzero frequency at long wavelength; the name does not guarantee visible-light interaction.
The distance along a wave from one point to the matching point in the next cycle, such as crest to crest.
For a repeating signal, the number of cycles per second. Five cycles each second is 5 hertz.

phonon-occupation.idea: A phonon is one energy step in a shared vibration pattern of atoms.
phonon-occupation.explanation: Each vibration pattern can gain energy in fixed-sized steps called phonons. Repeated measurements can find different whole-number counts, so their average need not be a whole number. Even zero phonons does not mean zero motion: the lowest quantum state retains zero-point energy.

example.title: One thermal mode
steps: Choose mode energy ε so that ε/(k_BT) = ln2.
Its mean phonon count is 1/(2−1) = 1, although individual measurements can give different counts.

terms.definition: The energy added by one phonon in this pattern.
Boltzmann's constant times positive kelvin temperature.
The exponential calculator function; exp(ln2) is 2.
The average phonon count.
Energy that remains in the lowest allowed vibration state.

lattice-heat-capacity.idea: At low temperature, many vibration modes are too costly to excite easily.
lattice-heat-capacity.explanation: Heat capacity measures how much energy changes per temperature rise. A simple three-dimensional Debye model predicts a lattice contribution proportional to T³ at low temperature. Electrons and other effects can add separate contributions.

example.title: Doubling temperature in the same regime
steps: The lattice heat capacity is 2 μJ/K at 5 K.
At 10 K the T³ model predicts 2 × 2³ = 16 μJ/K.

terms.definition: Energy change per temperature rise under stated conditions.
A simplified model of a solid's vibration modes.
One millionth of a joule.
Two quantities are proportional when multiplying one by a certain factor multiplies the other by that same factor.

pauli-box.idea: Electrons fill distinct complete states rather than all collecting in the lowest one.
pauli-box.explanation: A spatial state can offer two different spin states. Each complete spatial-and-spin state holds at most one electron. At zero temperature in this noninteracting model, fill the lowest energies first.

example.title: Four electrons in three levels
steps: Spatial levels have energies 1, 3 and 6 eV, each with two spin states.
Four electrons fill the first two levels, totaling 2 × 1 + 2 × 3 = 8 eV.

terms.definition: No two identical fermions occupy the same complete one-particle state.
An intrinsic quantum angular-momentum property.

density-of-states.idea: Available states and occupied states are different counts.
density-of-states.explanation: Density of states tells how many allowed states lie in an energy interval. Multiply by the interval width to estimate available states. Multiply by the occupation fraction as well to estimate how many are occupied.

example.title: One narrow energy interval
steps: Density of states is 40 states/eV across 0.10 eV, giving about four states.
If their occupation fraction is 0.25, the mean occupied count is one.

terms.definition: Available states per energy interval.
Average occupied fraction.
The narrow interval width.

fermi-occupancy.idea: Temperature softens the boundary between mostly occupied and mostly empty electron states.
fermi-occupancy.explanation: Chemical potential is the energy reference controlling equilibrium particle filling. At positive temperature, states well below it are mostly filled and states well above are mostly empty. Exactly at it, mean occupancy is one half.

example.title: A state at chemical potential
steps: Set E − μ = 0 at a positive temperature.
The exponential is one, giving occupancy 1/(1+1) = 0.50.

terms.definition: State energy.
Chemical potential.
Boltzmann's constant times kelvin temperature.
Average occupancy of one complete electron state.
A condition where the effects that would change the system balance. For a hanging weight at rest, the support’s upward pull balances gravity.
A function that changes by the same factor when its input changes by a fixed amount. For example, a signal that halves each second decays exponentially.

degenerate-gas.idea: A strongly filled electron gas does not follow dilute classical counting.
degenerate-gas.explanation: The Pauli rule blocks already occupied states. If temperature is far below the Fermi temperature, warming mainly changes states near the filling boundary. Here “degenerate” describes quantum statistics, not equal-energy levels.

example.title: A metal-like energy scale
steps: Fermi energy is 4 eV, giving Fermi temperature about 46400 K.
At 300 K the ratio is about 0.0065, so dilute classical occupancy is a poor model.

terms.definition: The zero-temperature filling energy measured from the band bottom.
That energy divided by Boltzmann's constant.
One amount divided by another. Three red counters for every two blue gives a red-to-blue ratio of 3/2.

bloch-form.idea: An electron wave can repeat its probability pattern while changing phase between cells.
bloch-form.explanation: A repeating crystal allows electron wave patterns whose shapes repeat from cell to cell. Their sign or wave-cycle stage can still change between repeats. Since probability depends on the amplitude's squared size, flipping its sign leaves the probability pattern unchanged.

example.title: A half-turn phase per cell
steps: Let ka = π, where a is cell spacing.
Moving one cell multiplies the amplitude by −1, but leaves its squared magnitude unchanged.

terms.definition: Electron wave amplitude; its squared size gives probability density.
Wave vector, measuring phase change per distance.
Cell spacing.
The imaginary-number unit used to describe a wave's cycle.
A factor describing the phase change over one cell.
A wave’s place in a repeating cycle. Two crests arriving together have matching phase.

A number used to combine quantum possibilities. For a single normalized reference state, square the size of its amplitude to get the chance of that outcome. For position, this gives a density that you add over a region.

nearly-free-gap.idea: A periodic potential can mix equal-energy waves and split their energies.
nearly-free-gap.explanation: An electron feels a repeating electric environment in a crystal. This can mix two wave patterns that originally had the same energy. The resulting combinations can have different energies, opening a gap: an interval with no allowed energy from these states.

example.title: A two-state split
steps: Use common energy 2.0 eV and coupling 0.15 eV.
The new energies are 1.85 and 2.15 eV, separated by 0.30 eV.

terms.definition: The supplied interaction energy mixing the two wave patterns.
The size of that interaction without its sign.
An interval between the split allowed energies.

tight-binding.idea: Coupling neighboring atomic states spreads one energy level into a band.
tight-binding.explanation: An electron's wave pattern can extend from one atomic site to its neighbors. This linking, called hopping in the model, makes different combinations have different energies and forms a band. It does not mean a classical electron jumps on a fixed schedule.

example.title: One point in a simple band
steps: Use E₀ = 1.0 eV and hopping t = 0.20 eV.
At k = 0, the model gives E = 1.0 − 0.40 = 0.60 eV.

terms.definition: The interaction energy linking neighboring states.
Wave vector, measuring phase change per distance.
Cell spacing.
Energy of an isolated site.
A range of allowed electron energies in a solid.

bandwidth-localization.idea: A narrow band shows weak coupling, but does not by itself prove localization.
bandwidth-localization.explanation: A narrow band, or small range of allowed energies, indicates weak linking between neighboring states in this model. A perfectly repeating chain can still allow waves spread across the whole chain. Disorder and interactions can instead concentrate states in a smaller region.

example.title: A weakly coupled chain
steps: Let the neighbor-linking energy have size 0.05 eV.
The simple band's width is 4 × 0.05 = 0.20 eV, but its allowed wave patterns can still extend across the ideal repeating chain.

terms.definition: The energy range covered by a band.
A state being concentrated in a limited spatial region.
Neighbor coupling energy.

filled-bands.idea: Electrons need accessible empty states to change their current response easily.
filled-bands.explanation: A filled ideal band has canceling current contributions, and its states are already occupied. A partly filled band has nearby empty states. This simple picture can be altered by interactions, disorder or strong fields.

example.title: A half-filled band
steps: At low temperature, an ideal band is only half occupied.
A weak field can rearrange occupation into nearby empty states more easily than in a full isolated band.

terms.definition: A range of allowed electron-state energies in a solid.
Which available states contain electrons.

fermi-surface.idea: Make a map of the wave patterns electrons can occupy in a metal. At zero temperature there is a boundary between filled and empty patterns.
fermi-surface.explanation: Each point on this map describes a wave’s direction and how quickly it repeats across space. The point is called a wave vector. For independent electrons the boundary at the highest filled energy is the Fermi surface. It belongs to the map of wave patterns.

example.title: A free-electron model
steps: States at the Fermi energy all have the same wave-vector magnitude.
Their directions form a sphere in three-dimensional wave-vector space.

terms.definition: The boundary between filled and empty states in the zero-temperature independent-electron model.
Wave vector.
The energy at the filling boundary.

group-effective-mass.idea: Band curvature determines how a wave packet responds to a weak force.
group-effective-mass.explanation: Electrons in a crystal respond to forces according to their allowed energy pattern. Near a rounded band minimum, the curve's bending determines a response number called effective mass. A more sharply bent curve gives a smaller effective mass in this simple approximation.

example.title: Two band minima
steps: The second parabolic minimum has twice the curvature of the first.
Its inverse effective mass doubles, so its effective mass is half as large.

terms.definition: A number describing how the electron wave packet accelerates under a weak force.
A localized combination of nearby wave patterns.
Planck's constant divided by 2π.
Wave vector, measuring wave-cycle change per distance.
The curvature, or bending, of the energy curve.
A result close enough to use when the stated conditions hold. For example, treating a nearly flat road as level can simplify a short-trip calculation.

drude-conductivity.idea: Conductivity depends on both carrier number and how easily carriers drift.
drude-conductivity.explanation: The Drude model treats scattering using one average relaxation time. An equivalent formula uses mobility, drift speed per electric field. More carriers do not guarantee high conductivity if their mobility is poor.

example.title: One carrier population
steps: Use density 2 × 10²² m⁻³, charge magnitude 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and mobility 0.05 m²/(V s).
The conductivity is 160 S/m.

terms.definition: Electrical conductivity.
Carrier number per volume.
Positive elementary charge.
Drift speed per electric-field strength.
A change in motion, direction or wave pattern after an interaction. A detector can record how much goes in each direction.
A rule for the force per unit positive charge at a place. Its direction is the way a small positive test charge would be pushed.

intrinsic-carriers.idea: Thermal excitation creates an electron and a hole together in an intrinsic semiconductor.
intrinsic-carriers.explanation: A semiconductor has filled electron states separated from higher available states by an energy gap. Heating can lift an electron across the gap, leaving a hole: an empty state that can also carry current. Without a donor or acceptor imbalance, each such excitation creates one electron and one hole.

example.title: A supplied thermal estimate
steps: Let √(N_cN_v) = 10²⁵ m⁻³ and E_g/(2k_BT) = 10.
The model gives equal electron and hole densities about 4.54 × 10²⁰ m⁻³.

terms.definition: Electron density.
Hole density.
Effective counts per volume of available states near the two band edges.
Band-gap energy.
Boltzmann's constant times positive kelvin temperature.
With no intentional donor or acceptor imbalance.

holes-charge.idea: Imagine a row of occupied seats with one empty seat. As people move into the gap one by one, the gap moves the other way.
holes-charge.explanation: Something similar happens when electrons move through a nearly full set of allowed states, called an energy band. The empty state is called a hole. Tracking its motion gives the same electric effect as a moving positive charge of size e.

example.title: Mobile-charge balance
steps: Hole density is 5 × 10²⁰ m⁻³ and electron density is 2 × 10²⁰ m⁻³.
Their mobile charge density is +48 C/m³ before fixed dopant charges are added.

terms.definition: An empty electron state in a nearly full band, treated as a positive carrier.
Hole density.
Electron density.

doping-chemical-potential.idea: Donor atoms can supply mobile electrons while leaving positive fixed charges behind.
doping-chemical-potential.explanation: Doping means deliberately adding impurity atoms to a semiconductor. Donors can release electrons into mobile states, becoming fixed positive ions. If nearly every donor is ionized and other carrier sources are negligible, mobile electron count is close to donor count.

example.title: Fully ionized donors
steps: There are 8 × 10²¹ donors per cubic metre, with negligible acceptors and intrinsic carriers.
The simple model gives electron density about 8 × 10²¹ m⁻³.

terms.definition: An impurity that can supply a mobile electron.
A donor left positively charged after releasing an electron.
Donor count per volume.
Mobile electron count per volume.

semiconductor-temperature.idea: A conductivity change can come from carrier density, mobility, or both.
semiconductor-temperature.explanation: Temperature can free carriers, create electron-hole pairs, or change scattering. Electron and hole currents both contribute. A conductivity curve alone therefore does not directly measure carrier density.

example.title: Two carrier contributions
steps: Use n = 10²², p = 10²⁰ m⁻³ and mobilities 0.10 and 0.04 m²/(V s).
With e ≈ 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, conductivity is about 160.64 S/m.

terms.definition: Electron and hole densities.
Their drift mobilities.
Conductivity.
A change in motion, direction or wave pattern after an interaction. A detector can record how much goes in each direction.

drift-diffusion.idea: A zero net current can hide equal and opposite drift and diffusion currents.
drift-diffusion.explanation: Diffusion spreads particles from crowded regions. Drift moves charged carriers in an electric field. These contributions can cancel even though particles keep moving randomly.

example.title: Electrons crowded toward the right
steps: Electrons diffuse left, giving conventional current to the right.
A leftward electric field can provide an equal leftward conventional drift current.

terms.definition: Spreading caused by random motion from higher to lower concentration.
The direction positive charge would flow.
Average directed carrier motion caused by a field.
A rule for the force per unit positive charge at a place. Its direction is the way a small positive test charge would be pushed.

depletion-region.idea: A junction's uncovered dopant ions create a field that opposes further carrier diffusion.
depletion-region.explanation: A p–n junction joins a hole-rich region with an electron-rich region. Carriers spread across and fill some empty states, uncovering fixed charged impurity ions. Their electric field resists further spreading. The side with fewer impurity ions needs a wider region to balance charge.

example.title: Unequal doping
steps: The acceptor density is four times the donor density.
Charge balance requires the n-side depletion width to be four times the p-side width.

terms.definition: The junction region with few mobile carriers but uncovered fixed impurity charge.
Acceptor and donor impurity counts per volume.
The depletion widths on the two sides.
A rule for the force per unit positive charge at a place. Its direction is the way a small positive test charge would be pushed.

diode-bias.idea: Forward bias lowers part of a junction's barrier and allows more current.
diode-bias.explanation: A p–n junction separates hole-rich material from electron-rich material. Making its p side more positive lowers the barrier resisting carrier flow; this is forward bias. The simple current rule rises rapidly, but real resistance and high carrier injection eventually change it.

example.title: A supplied forward bias
steps: Let eV/(n_idealk_BT) = ln3, so the exponential is 3.
The current is I_s(3−1) = 2I_s.

terms.definition: The model's positive reference current scale.
A fitted factor adjusting the exponential rise.
Boltzmann's constant times positive kelvin temperature.
Positive elementary charge.
Applied forward voltage.
The exponential calculator function.
A function that changes by the same factor when its input changes by a fixed amount. For example, a signal that halves each second decays exponentially.

photovoltaic-limits.idea: A solar cell converts only part of incoming light power into electrical power.
photovoltaic-limits.explanation: Light can create electron-hole pairs, and the junction helps separate and collect them. Some photons are not absorbed, and other energy becomes heat or is lost through recombination. Absorption alone is not efficiency.

example.title: One operating point
steps: A model cell receives 20 W of optical power and delivers 4 W electrically.
Its efficiency is 4/20 = 20%.

terms.definition: Useful output power divided by supplied input power.
An electron filling a hole rather than being collected.
One packet of electromagnetic radiation. Visible light and radio waves can both be described in photons.

dielectric-polarization.idea: An electric field can slightly separate bound positive and negative charge.
dielectric-polarization.explanation: Bound charges cannot travel freely through a dielectric, an insulating material. An electric field can still shift positive and negative charges slightly apart, making many tiny electric dipoles. Polarization counts their combined strength per volume; the response can depend on how rapidly the field changes.

example.title: A field doubles in one linear model
steps: In a supplied material model, electric susceptibility is 2, so polarization is P = 2ε₀E.
Doubling the applied field doubles the polarization if the same linear-response conditions hold.

terms.definition: Polarization, electric dipole moment per volume.
A separation of positive and negative charge.
Electric susceptibility, the material's linear response factor.
Vacuum permittivity, the electric constant.
Electric-field strength.
A rule for the force per unit positive charge at a place. Its direction is the way a small positive test charge would be pushed.

interband-absorption.idea: An electron needs the right energy and an available state to absorb light across bands.
interband-absorption.explanation: For a direct transition, the photon supplies the energy difference. The final state must be empty and the coupling allowed. Indirect transitions also involve a lattice vibration to balance momentum and energy.

example.title: A direct 2 eV gap
steps: A 1.5 eV photon cannot supply the required energy alone.
A 2 eV photon matches it, but absorption still needs an empty final state and allowed coupling.

terms.definition: A change between electron bands.
Planck's constant.
Light frequency.
One packet of electromagnetic radiation. Visible light and radio waves can both be described in photons.

excitons.idea: When an electron gains energy, it can leave an empty place behind. The electron and the empty place can travel as a pair.
excitons.explanation: The empty electron state is called a hole. It acts like a positive charge, so it attracts the negative electron. A bound pair is called an exciton. The extra energy needed to pull the two apart is the binding energy.

example.title: One bound pair
steps: The free-pair band gap is 2.0 eV and binding energy is 0.08 eV.
The exciton transition energy is approximately 1.92 eV.

terms.definition: A correlated, bound electron-hole pair in a material.

optical-evidence.idea: A spectral feature can support more than one material model.
optical-evidence.explanation: Compare the full prediction, not just a hoped-for peak. A residual is measurement minus prediction. Patterns in residuals can suggest missing physics or calibration problems, but even a good fit need not be unique.

example.title: One absorbance mismatch
steps: A model predicts 0.30 and the measurement is 0.36.
The residual is +0.06; a repeated nearby pattern deserves investigation rather than automatic dismissal as noise.

terms.definition: A logarithmic measure of how much light is removed from a beam; larger values mean less transmitted light.
Measured value minus predicted value.

magnetic-moments.idea: A magnetic moment aligned with a field has lower interaction energy in this simple model.
magnetic-moments.explanation: A magnetic moment describes how strongly something behaves like a tiny magnet and its direction. In the simple field-energy rule, lining up with the field lowers energy. Heat and quantum restrictions mean this does not force every moment to align perfectly.

example.title: Two orientations of one moment
steps: Let μB = 2 × 10⁻²³ J.
Parallel and antiparallel energies are −2 × 10⁻²³ and +2 × 10⁻²³ J, separated by 4 × 10⁻²³ J.

terms.definition: The magnetic moment's size.
Magnetic-field strength.
The angle between the moment and field.
Cosine, an angle function; it is 1 for parallel and −1 for opposite directions.

para-diamagnetism.idea: A material in a magnetic field can respond along the field or against it.
para-diamagnetism.explanation: Susceptibility measures how strongly the material responds. A small positive value means the response points along the field. A small negative value means it points the other way. For a dilute sample of independent tiny magnets, Curie’s rule predicts that doubling the absolute temperature halves its positive response.

example.title: Warming a sample of independent tiny magnets
steps: Its susceptibility is 0.004 at 200 K.
At 400 K, the same model predicts 0.002.

terms.definition: The material's linear magnetic-response factor.
The Curie constant for the sample.
Absolute temperature in kelvin.
A field that can turn a compass and push sideways on a moving electric charge.

exchange-order.idea: An effective interaction can favor parallel or opposite spin alignment.
exchange-order.explanation: Spin is a built-in quantum form of angular momentum, not literal ball-like rotation. Interactions can favor neighboring spins lining up together or oppositely. The sign of the supplied interaction rule tells which is favored; temperature and geometry also matter for a whole material.

example.title: A positive coupling
steps: Let J = 2 meV for classical unit spins.
Parallel energy is −2 meV and opposite energy is +2 meV, so parallel alignment is lower.

terms.definition: The interaction-energy factor linking the two spins.
The two classical unit-length spin arrows used in this toy comparison.
Their directional comparison: +1 when parallel, −1 when opposite.
One thousandth of an electronvolt.

domains-hysteresis.idea: A magnetic sample can contain ordered regions whose magnetizations cancel overall.
domains-hysteresis.explanation: A domain is a region with a common magnetization direction. A field can change domain sizes, while defects hinder their movement. The resulting dependence on past fields is called hysteresis.

example.title: Two unequal domains
steps: Three quarters of a sample points along +M₀ and one quarter along −M₀.
The net magnetization is (0.75−0.25)M₀ = 0.50M₀.

terms.definition: Magnetic moment per volume.
Response that depends on the system's earlier path.

superconducting-evidence.idea: Two clues can help identify a superconductor. One concerns current, and the other concerns magnetism.
superconducting-evidence.explanation: If a voltage meter reads zero while current flows, a tiny resistance could still be too small to see. Scientists also test how the sample responds to a magnetic field. Under suitable conditions a superconductor pushes magnetic field out of its interior. This is the Meissner effect. The strength of the applied field matters.

example.title: An instrument limit
steps: At current 1 mA, voltage is below a 1 nV resolution limit.
The measured bound is R < 10⁻⁶ Ω; a separate magnetic test is still needed.

terms.definition: Expulsion of bulk magnetic field in an appropriate equilibrium superconducting state.
A narrow region through which magnetic flux enters certain superconductors.
The smallest change an instrument can distinguish.
A field that can turn a compass and push sideways on a moving electric charge.

cooper-pairs.idea: In some very cold materials, electrons move in a shared state that includes linked pairs.
cooper-pairs.explanation: A metal’s atoms can vibrate. In a conventional superconductor, these vibrations can help link electrons near the highest occupied energy level. Two electrons linked this way form a Cooper pair. Their wave patterns can spread across many atoms and overlap other pairs.

example.title: A paired state spread across a metal
steps: In one conventional superconducting model, two linked electron wave patterns extend through many atomic spacings.
Other pairs occupy the same region too, so drawing each pair as an isolated two-electron orbit misrepresents the shared state.

terms.definition: Two electrons with linked quantum behavior in a superconducting description.
The energy boundary separating filled and empty electron states at zero temperature.
Here, a shared quantum state with a stable relationship among its wave-cycle stages.

gap-critical-scales.idea: In a simple fully gapped superconductor, creating excitations costs a minimum energy.
gap-critical-scales.explanation: An excitation is an added disturbance above the lowest-energy state. In a fully gapped superconductor, one such disturbance costs at least Δ. Breaking a pair creates two, costing about 2Δ. The displayed weak-coupling BCS rule connects this energy with transition temperature for a particular conventional model.

example.title: A 10 K transition temperature
steps: With T_c = 10 K, weak-coupling BCS gives 2Δ₀ ≈ 0.00303 eV.
Thus Δ₀ ≈ 0.00152 eV.

terms.definition: The minimum single-excitation energy at zero temperature.
The temperature where superconductivity appears in the model.
Boltzmann's constant.
A conventional electron-pairing theory named for Bardeen, Cooper and Schrieffer.

superconductor-limits.idea: Evidence of superconductivity does not make every superconducting model correct.
superconductor-limits.explanation: Zero resistance in one regime does not promise no losses at all currents, fields or frequencies. A model must also match the excitation pattern. A node is a place where the gap becomes zero.

example.title: A nodal sample
steps: Measurements support superconductivity but also show a gap that reaches zero in some directions.
A model predicting a nonzero gap everywhere cannot fully explain that spectrum.

terms.definition: A direction or point where the excitation gap becomes zero.
An added disturbance above the system's reference state.
The possible energies of disturbances above the lowest-energy state, shown here for different directions.

order-parameters.idea: An order parameter tracks the particular organization you want to study.
order-parameters.explanation: An order parameter is a chosen number that tracks organization. For a ferromagnet, a material whose moments can align together without an applied field, magnetization can serve this role. Oppositely aligned regions can cancel in the whole-sample average even though each region remains ordered.

example.title: One ordered domain
steps: Use reference magnetization 10⁶ A/m and measured domain magnetization 4 × 10⁵ A/m.
The normalized order parameter is 0.4.

terms.definition: Magnetic moment per volume.
A region with a common magnetization direction.
The chosen reference magnetization used for comparison.

correlation.idea: Two outcomes can be linked even when each has zero average.
correlation.explanation: Compare the average product with the product of separate averages. Their difference is a connected correlation. Zero for one chosen pair does not prove all outcomes are independent.

example.title: Always matching signs
steps: Half the trials give A = B = +1 and half give A = B = −1.
Both separate averages are zero, but AB is always one, so the correlation is one.

terms.definition: Average over repeated preparations.
A measure of how outcomes vary together.

band-topology.idea: Some global properties of band states resist small, smooth changes.
band-topology.explanation: Some band properties describe how electron wave states fit together across the whole wave-pattern map. A topological invariant is a label for one such global property. In the stated model, smooth changes cannot alter this label while the energy gap and required symmetry rules remain intact.

example.title: Connecting two supplied band models
steps: One model has invariant label 0 and another has label 1.
If we change the first smoothly into the second while keeping the required symmetry, the separating energy gap must close somewhere on that path.

terms.definition: A global label unchanged under the stated smooth, gap-preserving changes.
An interval separating the relevant allowed energies.
An allowed change that leaves the relevant physical rules unchanged.

many-body-prerequisites.idea: A useful simple model says what it keeps and what it leaves out.
many-body-prerequisites.explanation: A solid contains many interacting particles. Models simplify them into electron bands or shared vibration patterns, but each simplification leaves something out. A mismatch with data helps identify when another contribution or a more detailed model is needed.

example.title: An extra low-temperature heat contribution
steps: A model of lattice vibrations predicts heat capacity 2 microjoules per kelvin, while the measured value is 3 under the same conditions.
Investigate the extra contribution, including possible electron effects, before treating the vibration-only model as complete.

terms.definition: A range of allowed electron energies in a solid.
Energy needed for a temperature rise under specified conditions.
One millionth of a joule.
A unit of absolute temperature. Zero kelvin marks absolute zero. A change of one kelvin is the same size as a change of one degree Celsius.

band-occupancy-capstone.idea: A band diagram needs filling information before it can suggest transport behavior.
band-occupancy-capstone.explanation: Allowed energy ranges alone do not tell which states are occupied. A full lower band and empty upper band give one situation; available carriers in a partially filled band give another. Scattering and localization still matter.

example.title: A synthetic band gap
steps: The lower band ends at −1 eV and the upper starts at +1 eV.
The gap is 2 eV; it alone does not determine conductivity if the upper band is partly filled.

terms.definition: The energy interval between the stated band edges.
How strongly a material carries current in response to an electric field.
A change in motion, direction or wave pattern after an interaction. A detector can record how much goes in each direction.

transport-capstone.idea: One conductivity measurement cannot separately determine carrier density and mobility.
transport-capstone.explanation: The simple one-carrier model multiplies these quantities. A smaller density with larger mobility can give the same result. Convert square-centimetre mobility units carefully before using SI values.

example.title: Converting mobility
steps: Use density 5 × 10²² m⁻³ and mobility 200 cm²/(V s), or 0.020 m²/(V s).
With e ≈ 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, conductivity is 160 S/m.

terms.definition: Drift speed per electric-field strength.
Carrier density.
Conductivity.

thermal-electronic-capstone.idea: A measured heat capacity can combine electronic and lattice contributions.
thermal-electronic-capstone.explanation: In a limited low-temperature metal regime, a linear term models electrons and a cubic term models acoustic lattice vibrations. Add the contributions before comparing with data. A good fit still leaves room for other mechanisms.

example.title: Heat capacity at 2 K
steps: Use γ = 0.002 J/K² and β = 0.0001 J/K⁴.
The terms are 0.004 and 0.0008 J/K, totaling 0.0048 J/K.

terms.definition: The supplied linear heat-capacity coefficient.
The supplied cubic coefficient.
Kelvin temperature.
The energy needed for a temperature rise of one kelvin under the stated conditions, with no change of phase.

materials-assessment.idea: A treated crystal can scatter light differently and also carry less current. Those two changes alone do not tell you what caused them.
materials-assessment.explanation: A shifted scattering peak can mean the spacing between crystal planes changed. If the number of moving charges per volume stayed the same, lower conductivity can mean they move less easily. This second inference assumes one kind of charge carrier. Check other possible changes in the sample too.

example.title: One processed sample
steps: For the same reflection, sinθ rises from 0.50 to 0.55, so spacing becomes about 0.909 of its old value.
Conductivity falls to 0.70 at independently unchanged carrier density, suggesting mobility also falls to 0.70.
These separate inferences do not establish that contraction caused the mobility loss.

terms.definition: Drift speed per electric-field strength.
A conclusion drawn from evidence using stated assumptions.
The spreading of a wave when it passes through an opening or around an edge.
